extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers of literature interested in Gabriel García Márquez
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and summarize the literary techniques, themes, and production practices attributed to Gabriel García Márquez as described on his Wikipedia page. Useful for literary analysis, creative-writing study, or emulating aspects of his style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit seemingly important details to invite reader participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave out seemingly important details and events so the reader is forced into a more participatory role in the story development (example: in No One Writes to the Colonel the main characters are not given names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspired by Greek tragedy (events occur off-stage); omission should be deliberate to engage readers' imagination rather than from negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let style be determined by subject and mood
rubrics_metrics.description: The style is determined by the subject, by the mood of the times. If you try to use something that is not suitable, it just won't work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose register, tone, and formal devices that fit the theme and historical/psychological mood of the piece rather than forcing a preconceived style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the extraordinary as perfectly natural (deadpan delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present magical, superstitious or supernatural elements in a deadpan, matter-of-fact way so that the fantastic reads as part of ordinary reality (influence traced to his grandmother's storytelling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid special effects or heightened commentary when presenting odd events; the narrative voice should normalize the fantastic to preserve verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine the fantastic and the realistic (magical realism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use magical elements and events in otherwise ordinary and realistic situations so that 'the fantastic and the realistic are combined in a richly composed world of imagination' (Nobel citation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate fantastical occurrences seamlessly into social, historical, or domestic detail rather than segregating them as allegory or pure fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin from a visual image; use visual/graphic language
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story is often inspired by 'a visual image' and critics describe his language as visual or graphic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground scenes and moments in striking visual details; this also helps work adapt well to film or cinematic description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a setting as a symbolic 'state of mind' (Macondo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a fictional setting that functions beyond specific geography—Macondo is described as 'not so much a place as a state of mind'—allowing the setting to capture general regional myth and thematic resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep some specificity (regional color) but allow ambiguity so the place serves as symbolic or allegorical terrain across works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use journalistic methods and reportage in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate journalistic investigation, reportage techniques, and factual-seeming detail into narrative fiction (examples: Chronicle of a Death Foretold, News of a Kidnapping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ interviews, documentary detail, and the reporter's reconstructive stance to lend credibility and procedural texture to fiction; balance factual tone with imaginative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interweave characters and motifs across works
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat characters, situations, and motifs across different stories and novels (e.g., characters from One Hundred Years of Solitude reappear in other works), creating a cohesive literary universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurring figures and places to build continuity and resonance; vary perspective so repetition deepens rather than bores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore solitude as a central thematic concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme of solitude runs through much of his work, exploring the solitude of individuals and humanity, and connecting it to broader regional or historical experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weave solitude into character motivation, social contexts, and narrative consequences rather than treating it as incidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ non-linear or inverted narrative structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure plots in non-chronological or inverted fashions (example: Chronicle of a Death Foretold 'moves backward' rather than forward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporal disruption strategically to foreground memory, investigation, or thematic pattern rather than as gratuitous complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stream-of-consciousness and interior perspective when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ stream-of-consciousness techniques to convey interior experience (example: Leaf Storm follows a child's stream of consciousness exploring death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt interior techniques to the psychological aims of the passage; ensure voice and syntactic choices support readability and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base formal structure on modernist techniques and literary influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw on modernist formal devices and named influences (e.g., In Evil Hour's formal structure based on Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway; Faulkner's narrative techniques influenced him).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and adapt structural models (episodic, shifting focalization, associative time) but make them serve your subjects and regional inflections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real events as a point of departure but fictionalize freely
rubrics_metrics.description: Start from real incidents (journalistic cases, historical events) but maintain that little beyond the point of departure remains literal—fictionalize characters, motives, and structure (Chronicle of a Death Foretold as an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the feel of factuality while taking imaginative liberties to explore theme and meaning ethically (acknowledge sources where appropriate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate political and historical reality into fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference and embed political/historical phenomena (e.g., La Violencia, banana company episodes, dictatorships) within narratives to ground magical-realist worlds in sociohistorical conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let political context inform character choices and communal dynamics; avoid reducing politics to mere backdrop—it should shape stakes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain disciplined, intensive writing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Commit to sustained, daily writing for extended periods (example: García Márquez wrote every day for 18 months to complete One Hundred Years of Solitude, selling his car to support his family).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat long-form projects as requiring concentrated, disciplined work rhythms; practical sacrifices and routine can be part of the production strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose novels as richly textured imaginative worlds reflecting life and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a 'richly composed world of imagination' that reflects a continent's life and conflicts by combining intense imagination with grounded social observation (as noted in Nobel citation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance lyrical or fantastic elements with ethnographic, historical, and emotional specificity so the invented world feels socially and morally invested.
